question: What does the padlock next to a web address actually tell you?
options: The site is legit and safe
why: Only that the link is encrypted. Nearly all phishing sites show a padlock too, so it says nothing about honesty.

question: SMS: 'Your SARS refund is ready, tap the link to confirm bank details.' True?
options: SARS sends refund links in tax season
Fine if it quotes your tax number
SARS never sends links to other sites
why: SARS says it never sends hyperlinks or asks for banking details by SMS. Open eFiling yourself to check a refund.

question: Caller ID shows your bank's number. They ask for your OTP 'to stop fraud'.
options: Hang up: caller ID can be faked
Share it: the number is verified
Share it if they know your ID number
why: Caller ID is easy to spoof, and an OTP approves a transaction. SABRIC: never give an OTP over the phone, to anyone.

question: A QR sticker on a parking meter opens a payment page. Main risk?
options: A fake sticker over the real code
why: A QR code is just a link. Crooks stick their own codes over real ones so you pay them. Check the address first.

question: Friend's WhatsApp: 'Sent you a 6-digit code by mistake, forward it.' If you do?
options: They only see your old backups
why: It's your WhatsApp registration code. Whoever has it moves your account to their phone, then scams your contacts.

question: LinkedIn recruiter: remote job, but first pay R1 500 for training and a laptop.
options: A scam: real employers don't charge
Fine if refunded with first salary
why: Real employers don't make you pay to get hired. Paying for 'training' or 'equipment' is the classic job-scam ask.

question: Phone says 'No service' for hours; people beside you have signal. Biggest worry?
options: A SIM swap to grab your OTPs
why: Crooks move your number to their SIM to receive your bank OTPs. Unexplained signal loss: call your network now.

question: Which of these is true two-factor sign-in?
options: Password + code sent to your phone
why: Two factors means two different kinds: something you know plus something you have. A question is just another password.

question: Open airport Wi-Fi, your bank's real HTTPS site. Can others read your password?
options: Only if you're not in incognito
why: HTTPS encrypts it end to end. The bigger Wi-Fi risk today is being sent to a fake login page, not someone reading traffic.

question: You log in on a perfect fake bank site. Which factor still saves you?
why: Codes can be typed into the fake site and relayed in seconds. A passkey only works on the real site it was made for.

question: Windows 10 support ended Oct 2025. Without paid updates, what stopped?
why: The PC still runs and Defender definitions continue to 2028, but holes in Windows itself no longer get patched.

question: Besides remembering passwords, how does a password manager fight phishing?
options: It won't autofill on a fake site
why: It fills only on the real site's address. If it won't autofill, stop: you may be on a lookalike page.

question: 3-2-1 backups: 3 copies, 2 types of storage, and 1 copy…
why: One copy away from the building survives fire, theft, and ransomware that hits everything on your network.

question: Supplier emails from their real address: 'New bank account, pay here.' Best step?
options: Reply to the email to confirm
Call them on a number you already have
why: Real mailboxes get hacked, so a reply reaches the crook. Verify bank changes by phone, on a number from your own records.

question: 2 am: fifteen 'Approve sign-in?' prompts you didn't trigger. Most likely meaning?
why: 'MFA fatigue': a crook with your password spams prompts hoping you tap Approve. Deny them, then change the password.

question: Your CEO's exact voice: 'Urgent payment, I'm boarding, just do it.' Best check?
options: Hang up, call his known number
Ask him to confirm by email
why: Voices clone from seconds of audio, and email and caller ID can be faked. Call back on a number you already have.

question: Under POPIA, 'personal information' can be about whom?
options: Only people with SA ID numbers
why: Unlike GDPR, POPIA also covers identifiable, existing juristic persons such as companies, not just people.

question: A Google sign-in pop-up shows the right address. Can it still be fake?
options: No, the address bar proves it
Yes, the page can draw the whole window
why: 'Browser-in-the-browser' draws a fake pop-up, address bar and all. Tell: your password manager won't autofill it.

question: Fake app got 'Allow' access to your mail. Does a password reset fix it?
options: Yes, it locks the app out
Yes, if MFA is switched on
why: The app got its own access, no password needed. Resets and MFA don't touch it: remove the app's permission.

question: POPIA breach: who must the company notify, and when?
why: Section 22: the Regulator and the people affected, as soon as reasonably possible. 72 hours is GDPR's rule, not POPIA's.

question: Staffer emails a client list to the wrong person. Report it under POPIA?
options: No, if the email was recalled
why: The Information Regulator says POPIA has no threshold: every security compromise, low risk included, gets reported.

question: Researchers dropped ~300 USB sticks on campus. Files were opened on roughly…
why: About 45%, the first within 6 minutes, mostly by people trying to return it. Hand found drives to IT, unplugged.

question: NIST's current advice on forcing password changes every 90 days?
why: Forced changes breed weak, predictable passwords. NIST says don't, but force a change when there's evidence of compromise.

question: You pay a ransomware gang to delete your stolen data. Assume what?
options: It's deleted: gangs keep their word
Copies may still exist and resurface
why: Responders have seen 'deleted' data leaked or used to extort again after payment. Paying buys a promise, not deletion.

question: An attacker steals the krbtgt hash. What can they now forge?
why: That's a Golden Ticket: with krbtgt they mint Kerberos tickets for any account in the domain. Reset krbtgt twice.

question: Hundreds of Windows Security event 4625 in a minute. What are you seeing?
why: 4625 = an account failed to log on. A burst of them is brute force or password spraying (4720 = account created, 4698 = task).

question: Which DMARC policy tells receivers to refuse mail spoofing your domain?
why: p=reject asks receivers to reject mail failing DMARC, ideally during SMTP. p=quarantine only marks it suspicious; p=none just monitors.
